candidates.attacker_control: A consuming Sling application passes an attacker-controlled URL (e.g., an href/src value from a request parameter or content property) to XSSAPI.getValidHref(), which is the documented sanitizer for writing URLs into HTML href/src attributes.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Checked whether the policy-provided href attribute (config.xml:808 references the common 'href' attribute at 244-248) could be stricter than the code fallback: its onsiteURL/offsiteURL regexes (config.xml:69-72) are the same patterns as DEFAULT_HREF_ATTRIBUTE, so the payload also passes with the repository policy rather than the fallback. Checked the colon requirement: the payload contains no literal ':', only the entity :, so the second regex (http/ftp/mailto) is not needed and the onsiteURL alternative is sufficient. Checked uncertainty about AntiSamy's matchesAllowedExpression() semantics: the payload passes under either full-match or find() semantics because every character in it belongs to the allowed class. Counterevidence/limitation: if a caller additionally HTML-escapes the returned value (turning '&' into '&'), the payload would not execute; and the certificate is source-level only, not runtime-verified.
candidates.impact: Cross-site scripting in applications relying on this API: script execution in the victim's browser origin when the crafted link is activated, i.e., the XSS protection API returns a value it advertises as safe but which the browser interprets as a javascript: URL. Depending on callers, potentially reflected or stored XSS.
candidates.prerequisites: 1) A Sling application uses XSSAPI.getValidHref() as the sole sanitizer for user-supplied URLs and writes the result into an HTML attribute without re-escaping it (this is the method's documented contract: 'Sanitizes a URL for writing as an HTML href or src attribute value'). 2) A victim activates the resulting link. 3) The AntiSamy policy's a/href attribute (or the hard-coded fallback) is used, as analyzed.
candidates.root_cause: XSSAPIImpl.getValidHref() neutralizes HTML-context metacharacters by percent-encoding only '"', "'", '>', '<', '`', space and ':' after '?', but never neutralizes the HTML character-reference metacharacters '&', '#' and ';'. The href validators it relies on (XSSFilterImpl.isValidHref() against the policy href attribute, or the fallback DEFAULT_HREF_ATTRIBUTE copied from AntiSamy) use AntiSamy's onsiteURL/offsiteURL regexes, whose first alternative full-matches a character class that explicitly includes '&', '#', ';', '(', ')', digits and letters. An entity-encoded scheme payload therefore passes every check and is returned verbatim.
candidates.title: getValidHref() allow-list accepts HTML entity-encoded javascript: URLs (XSS bypass)
candidates.trace: Input 'javascript:alert(1)': (a) the replaceAll chain at XSSAPIImpl.java:200-205 makes no change (no quotes, angle brackets, backtick or space); (b) indexOf('?') is -1 so the query-string colon encoding at 206-209 is skipped; (c) mangleNamespaces() (152-188) finds no '://' and no ':' and returns the string unchanged; (d) XSSFilterImpl.isValidHref() (243-251) checks the policy href attribute: containsAllowedValue() is false (no literal values), but matchesAllowedExpression() succeeds because the onsiteURL regex at config.xml:70 (identical to DEFAULT_HREF_ATTRIBUTE at XSSFilterImpl.java:61) full-matches digits, letters, '&', '#', ';', '(' and ')'; (e) getValidHref() returns the entity-encoded string unchanged. The browser subsequently decodes j to 'j' and : to ':' inside the attribute value, yielding the URL javascript:alert(1).
candidates.unverified: AntiSamy's Attribute.matchesAllowedExpression() implementation (embedded library not in this snapshot) and exact consuming-caller behavior were not verifiable here; the final 'browser decodes character references in attribute values' step is standard HTML behavior but not exercised at runtime in this review. No build, tests, or exploit execution were performed.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-79 Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation (XSS) / sanitizer bypass

coverage_summary: Source scope: 19 files, 13 Java (152 indexed symbols, 217 call sites, 224 relation edges; index reports 13/13 Java files parsed, 0 omissions, but no control-flow, data-flow or semantic resolution). I read all impl classes (XSSFilterImpl, XSSAPIImpl, PolicyHandler, HtmlToHtmlContentContext, PlainTextToHtmlContentContext, XSSFilterRule, LongValidationRule, XSSAPIAdapterFactory) and the API types (XSSFilter, ProtectionContext) in full, XSSAPI.java partially (lines 1-120 plus targeted searches), JSONUtil in full, and package-info not read. pom.xml, README.md and validation.properties were read; config.xml (106 KB) was reviewed through targeted searches (script/style/href/onsiteURL/offsiteURL/event attributes) rather than in full; ESAPI.properties was examined via searches only. No tests exist in the scope and none were run; no binaries or generated files are present.
limitations: Findings are static source-level leads; no code was executed, no build or test run, and no runtime/exploit verification was performed.

The embedded AntiSamy and OWASP Encoder/ESAPI libraries are dependencies, not part of the snapshot; their exact validation semantics (e.g., Attribute.matchesAllowedExpression, MagicSAXFilter entity decoding) could not be inspected and were reasoned about from their regexes in config.xml and from comments.

Reachability and exploitability depend on external Sling applications that call XSSAPI; no in-repo callers of getValidHref/getValidXML exist (this is a library bundle), so end-to-end data flow could not be traced inside the snapshot.
config.xml (106 KB) and ESAPI.properties were not read line-by-line; other policy-based weaknesses (e.g., CSS style-attribute scanning behavior) may remain uninspected.
The P1 relation index provides syntactic navigation only (no control/data flow, no semantic resolution, unresolved calls), so index edges were not treated as proof of behavior.
Version/branch context (pom version 1.0.8) suggests later upstream fixes may exist, but no patch, CVE, or ground-truth data was consulted or is available in this run.

rejected_leads.lead: Blind XXE in XSSAPIImpl.getValidXML() (lines 353-372): SAXParserFactory is created in activate() (lines 62-68) with only setValidating(false)/setNamespaceAware(true); no disallow-doctype-decl or external-entity hardening, and reader.parse(new InputSource(new StringReader(xml))) parses caller-supplied XML.
rejected_leads.reason: Plausible CWE-611, but the parsed document is not returned (only the original string on success), so impact is blind/out-of-band (SSRF or file access whose content is only surfaced in debug logs); exploitability depends on JDK parser defaults and on a caller passing untrusted XML, and no in-repo evidence ties it to a specific fix. Kept as a secondary lead, not the selected candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: CSS injection concerns in getValidStyleToken()/getValidCSSColor()/getValidMultiLineComment() (XSSAPIImpl.java:275-316): permissive CSS token regexes (e.g., unquoted url() values, tab characters inside quoted strings due to the case-insensitive 'javascript\s?:' lookahead, comment values only checked for '*/').
rejected_leads.reason: Depends heavily on how a caller embeds the returned token and on legacy-browser CSS behavior; no source-level end-to-end sink is visible in this repository, so the evidence threshold for a distinct candidate was not met.

rejected_leads.lead: mangleNamespaces() builds a replacement string from attacker-controlled group(1) and calls Matcher.appendReplacement() (XSSAPIImpl.java:171-182), which can throw IllegalArgumentException on '$' followed by an out-of-range group number.
rejected_leads.reason: Worst case appears to be an uncaught runtime exception (local denial of service) in getValidHref for crafted input; impact and confidence are much weaker than the selected href bypass.

rejected_leads.lead: XSSFilterImpl.updateDefaultHandler()/handleEvent() load the AntiSamy policy from repository content at /libs/sling/xss/config.xml (XSSFilterImpl.java:84-157).
rejected_leads.reason: This is an intentional administrative override mechanism; it requires content-write privileges on that path, so it is a privilege/configuration assumption rather than an attacker-controlled vulnerability in this snapshot.

rejected_leads.lead: PlainTextToHtmlContentContext.escapeXml() escapes only '&', '<' and '>' (lines 50-69), and JSONUtil writes raw values alongside _xss variants (JSONUtil.java:67-71, 141-152).
rejected_leads.reason: These match the declared contexts (HTML text content; an explicitly documented raw-plus-protected JSON convention) and no attribute/JS context misuse is present in-repo.

summary: Reviewed the Apache Sling XSS bundle snapshot (13 Java files, AntiSamy policy config.xml, ESAPI config). The strongest source-supported issue is an HTML-entity bypass in XSSAPI.getValidHref(): the href allow-list regexes explicitly permit '&', '#' and ';', and getValidHref only percent-encodes \", ', >, <, ` and space (plus ':' after '?'), so an entity-encoded javascript: URL such as javascript:alert(1) is returned unchanged as a "valid href". When a consuming application writes that value into an HTML attribute, the browser decodes the character references and obtains a javascript: URL, defeating the sanitizer (XSS). Other suspects (blind XXE in getValidXML, CSS-token/style comment concerns, mangleNamespaces exception) were considered and are recorded as rejected/unconfirmed leads. No runtime verification was performed; findings are source-level leads only.
